pairs.source_text: Ne quis miretur qui sim, paucis eloquar. ego Lar sum familiaris ex hac familia unde exeuntem me aspexistis.
pairs.question: Quis deus prologum Aululariae Plauti agit?
pairs.question_en: What god speaks the prologue of Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: Canonical literary fact: the Aulularia's prologue is spoken by the household Lar — Roman domestic religion stepping through the Greek mask to open the play. One-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: sed mi avos huius obsecrans concredidit thensaurum auri clam omnis: in medio foco defodit, venerans me ut id servarem sibi.
pairs.question: Quo loco avus Euclionis thensaurum auri defoderat, ut Lar in Aululariae prologo narrat?
pairs.question_en: Where had Euclio's grandfather buried the treasure of gold, as the Lar tells in the prologue of the Aulularia?
pairs.answer_en: In the middle of the hearth.
pairs.derivation: The treasure entrusted to the Lar and buried in the hearth — the focus being precisely the Lar's seat in the Roman house. Anchored to Euclio's grandfather + the Lar; one-place answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: huic filia una est. ea mihi cottidie aut ture aut vino aut aliqui semper supplicat, dat mihi coronas.
pairs.question: Quibus donis filia Euclionis Larem familiarem cottidie colit, ut ipse Lar apud Plautum narrat?
pairs.question_en: With what gifts does Euclio's daughter honor the household Lar every day, as the Lar himself tells in Plautus?
pairs.derivation: Roman household cult in daily practice: incense, wine, and garlands offered to the Lar — the standard domestic offerings. Anchored to Euclio's daughter + the Lar; three-item answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: eius honoris gratia feci, thensaurum ut hic reperiret Euclio, quo illam facilius nuptum, si vellet, daret.
pairs.question: Cuius honoris gratia Lar familiaris effecit, ut Euclio thensaurum reperiret?
pairs.answer: Filiae Euclionis, quae eum cottidie colebat.
pairs.question_en: For whose sake did the household Lar bring it about that Euclio found the treasure?
pairs.answer_en: For Euclio's daughter, who worshipped him daily.
pairs.derivation: The Lar's stated motive: he reveals the treasure to reward the pious daughter and provide her a dowry — the theology of the household cult (honor repaid) driving the plot. Anchored to the Lar + Euclio; short answer verbatim in substance.

pairs.source_text: is adulescentis illius est avonculus, qui illam stupravit noctu, Cereris vigiliis.
pairs.question: Quo festo tempore filia Euclionis in Aulularia Plauti vitiata est?
pairs.question_en: At what festival time was Euclio's daughter violated in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.answer_en: At night, during the vigil of Ceres.
pairs.derivation: Named rite anchoring the plot: the nocturnal vigil of Ceres, at which Lyconides assaulted the girl. Festival knowledge (criterion 8) with a one-phrase answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Aulam repertam auri plenam Euclio Vi summa servat, miseris adfectus modis.
pairs.question: Quam rem Euclio senex avarus in Aulularia Plauti summa vi servat?
pairs.question_en: What does the miserly old man Euclio guard with all his might in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: The title-fact of the play: Euclio the miser and his aula (pot) of gold, from which the Aulularia is named — the canonical literature-fact every Latin reader carries. Short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam noster nostrae qui est magister curiae dividere argenti dixit nummos in viros
pairs.question: Quis, ut Euclio in Aulularia Plauti refert, nummos argenti in viros dividere dixerat?
pairs.question_en: Who, as Euclio reports in Plautus' Aulularia, had announced a distribution of silver coins per man?
pairs.derivation: Roman civic institution through the Greek mask: the curia and its magister distributing a money dole man by man — the errand that forces Euclio from home. One-office answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Post mediam aetatem qui media ducit uxorem domum, si eam senex anum praegnatem fortuito fecerit, quid dubitas, quin sit paratum nomen puero Postumus?
pairs.question: Quod nomen puero paratum esse Megadorus in Aulularia iocatur, quem senex ex anu uxore genuerit?
pairs.question_en: What name does Megadorus in the Aulularia joke is ready-made for a boy begotten by an old man on an aged wife?
pairs.derivation: Roman naming custom: Postumus, the cognomen for the late-born (or after-born) child, deployed as the punchline of Megadorus' joke about old men marrying. Anchored to Megadorus; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: istas magnas factiones, animos, dotes dapsiles, clamores, imperia, eburata vehicla, pallas, purpuram, nil moror quae in servitutem sumptibus redigunt viros.
pairs.question: Quo uxores magnis cum dotibus viros suos redigere Megadorus apud Plautum dicit?
pairs.question_en: To what condition does Megadorus in Plautus say wives with great dowries reduce their husbands?
pairs.derivation: Megadorus' famous tirade on dowered wives — their retinues, ivory carriages, mantles and purple enslave the husband. A mores locus classicus on the Roman dowry debate; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: hoc magnum est periclum, ab asinis ad boves transcendere.
pairs.question: Quid Euclio in Aulularia Plauti magnum periculum esse dicit, cum de nuptiis cum divite loquitur?
pairs.question_en: What does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia say is a great danger, speaking of marriage with a rich man?
pairs.answer_en: To climb over from the asses to the oxen.
pairs.derivation: Proverbial saying the play made famous: the poor man 'crossing from asses to oxen' (marrying above his station) courts ruin. Quoted verbatim per the proverb rule; anchored to Euclio.

pairs.source_text: altera manu fert lapidem, panem ostentat altera.
pairs.question: Quid altera manu fert, qui panem altera ostentat, secundum proverbium apud Plautum in Aulularia?
pairs.question_en: What does he carry in one hand who shows bread with the other, according to the proverb in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: The proverb of the two-faced benefactor — bread on show, stone in hand — coined of the rich man flattering the poor. Quoted point is checkable; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ego istos novi polypos, qui ubi quidquid tetigerunt tenent.
pairs.question: Quibus animalibus Euclio in Aulularia Plauti divites comparat, qui quidquid tetigerunt tenent?
pairs.question_en: To what animals does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia compare the rich, who hold whatever they have touched?
pairs.derivation: Proverbial image: the grasping man as a polypus that never lets go of what it touches. Anchored to Euclio + the rich; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Mirum quin tua me causa faciat Iuppiter Philippum regem aut Dareum, trivenefica.
pairs.question: Quos duos reges Euclio in Aulularia Plauti ut exempla summarum divitiarum nominat?
pairs.question_en: Which two kings does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia name as bywords for the greatest wealth?
pairs.derivation: Philip of Macedon and Darius of Persia as proverbially rich kings — the shared byword for fabulous wealth (cf. the Philippei nummi). Two-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: cultrum, securim, pistillum, mortarium, quae utenda vasa semper vicini rogant, fures venisse atque abstulisse dicito.
pairs.question: Quae quattuor vasa vicinos semper utenda rogare Euclio in Aulularia Plauti dicit?
pairs.question_en: What four utensils does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia say the neighbors are always asking to borrow?
pairs.answer_en: The knife, the axe, the pestle, and the mortar.
pairs.derivation: Daily-life custom: the standing neighborly loan of kitchen implements (vasa utenda), the four named items being the stock list. Anchored to Euclio + the neighbors; four-item answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: interea senex Megadorus a sorore suasus ducere uxorem avari gnatam deposcit sibi.
pairs.question: A qua persuasus Megadorus senex uxorem ducere in Aulularia Plauti statuit?
pairs.question_en: By whom was the old man Megadorus persuaded to take a wife in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: Named relation of the plot: Megadorus moves to marry at his sister's urging (Eunomia in the play). Anchored to Megadorus; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid nunc? etiam mihi despondes filiam? Illis legibus, cum illa dote quam tibi dixi. Sponden ergo? Spondeo.
pairs.question: Quo verbo sollemni Euclio filiam suam Megadoro in Aulularia Plauti despondet?
pairs.question_en: With what solemn word does Euclio betroth his daughter to Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: The Roman betrothal by sponsio — the formal question-and-answer 'sponden? / spondeo' — enacted on stage. Roman law of engagement through the Greek mask; one-word answer verbatim. Speaker tags stripped per normalization.

pairs.source_text: At nihil est dotis quod dem. Ne duas. dum modo morata recte veniat, dotata est satis.
pairs.question: Qua re satis dotatam esse virginem Megadorus in Aulularia Plauti dicit, etiam sine pecunia?
pairs.question_en: With what does Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia say a girl is sufficiently dowered, even without money?
pairs.derivation: The famous sententia on dowries: 'dum modo morata recte veniat, dotata est satis' — character as dowry, the moral counterpart to Megadorus' anti-dowry tirade. Short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tun, trium litterarum homo, me vituperas? fur.
pairs.question: Quis appellatur 'trium litterarum homo' apud Plautum in Aulularia?
pairs.question_en: Who is called 'a man of three letters' in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.answer_en: A thief (fur — spelled with three letters).
pairs.derivation: The celebrated 'trium litterarum homo' joke: the three letters are f-u-r, 'thief' — a proverbial tag the play made famous, hurled by one cook at the other. Kept per instructions as a famous checkable saying; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cocus ille nundinalest, in nonum diem solet ire coctum.
pairs.question: Quoto quoque die cocus 'nundinalis' coctum ire solet, ut Anthrax in Aulularia Plauti iocatur?
pairs.question_en: Every how many days does the 'market-day cook' go out to cook, as Anthrax jokes in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: The Roman nundinae — the ninth-day market cycle — underlie the joke of the cook hired only once a market-week. Calendar realia through the Greek mask; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Postquam obsonavit erus et conduxit coquos tibicinasque hasce apud forum, edixit mihi ut dispertirem obsonium hic bifariam.
pairs.question: Vbi Megadorus coquos tibicinasque in nuptias conduxit, ut in Aulularia Plauti narratur?
pairs.question_en: Where did Megadorus hire the cooks and the flute-girls for the wedding, as told in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: Roman wedding logistics: cooks and tibicinae hired in the forum, with the provisions (obsonium), for a nuptial feast — daily-life custom evidenced verbatim. One-place answer.

pairs.source_text: Vicini huius Euclionis senis e proximo. ei adeo obsoni hinc iussit dimidium dari, cocum alterum itidemque alteram tibicinam.
pairs.question: Quantam obsonii partem Megadorus ad Euclionem in nuptias mitti iussit apud Plautum?
pairs.answer: Dimidium, cum altero coco et altera tibicina.
pairs.question_en: How large a share of the provisions did Megadorus order sent to Euclio for the wedding, in Plautus?
pairs.answer_en: Half, with one of the two cooks and one of the two flute-girls.
pairs.derivation: The rich groom underwrites the poor father-in-law's share of the feast, split 'bifariam' — wedding custom and the play's plot engine. Short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: i sane cum illo, Phrugia. tu autem, Eleusium, huc intro abi ad nos.
pairs.question: Quibus nominibus duae tibicinae in Aulularia Plauti appellantur?
pairs.question_en: By what names are the two flute-girls in Plautus' Aulularia called?
pairs.derivation: The named tibicinae of the wedding — the hired flute-girl being a fixture of Roman festivity (and of the comic stage). Anchored to the play; two-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tu, Congrio, quem illic reliquit agnum, eum sume atque abi intro illuc
pairs.question: Vter coquorum in Aulularia Plauti ad aedes Euclionis coquere missus est?
pairs.question_en: Which of the two cooks in Plautus' Aulularia was sent to cook at Euclio's house?
pairs.derivation: The canonical cook Congrio (named for the conger eel) drawn by lot to the miser's house, where Euclio cudgels him — a scene every reader of the play carries. One-name answer verbatim; editorial brackets stripped.

pairs.source_text: Quia ad tris viros iam ego deferam nomen tuom. Quam ob rem? Quia cultrum habes.
pairs.question: Ad quos magistratus Euclio nomen Congrionis coqui deferre minatur, quia cultrum habet?
pairs.question_en: To which magistrates does Euclio threaten to report the cook Congrio's name, because he carries a knife?
pairs.answer_en: To the tresviri (the Roman police board of three).
pairs.derivation: Roman policing through the Greek mask: carrying a blade gets you denounced to the tresviri capitales — the same anachronistic board Sosia fears in the Amphitruo. One-office answer verbatim; speaker tags stripped.

pairs.source_text: pulmentum pridem ei eripuit milvos: homo ad praetorem plorabundus devenit; infit ibi postulare plorans, eiulans, ut sibi liceret milvom vadarier.
pairs.question: Ad quem magistratum Euclio plorabundus devenit, cum milvus ei pulmentum eripuisset, ut in Aulularia iocose narratur?
pairs.question_en: To which magistrate did Euclio come weeping when a kite had snatched his food, as jokingly told in the Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: Roman legal anachronism in Greek dress: the miser asks the praetor for leave to summon the kite to court (vadari — the formal vadimonium). Anchored to Euclio + the praetor; one-office answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ita me bene amet Laverna, uti te iam, nisi reddi mihi vasa iubes, pipulo hic differam ante aedis.
pairs.question: Quam deam Congrio cocus in Aulularia Plauti iurans invocat?
pairs.question_en: Which goddess does the cook Congrio invoke in his oath in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: Laverna, the Roman goddess of thieves, sworn by — aptly — a cook, the proverbially light-fingered trade. Roman popular religion evidenced verbatim; one-name answer. Editorial brackets stripped.

pairs.source_text: Cererin, Pythodice, has sunt facturi nuptias? Qui? Quia temeti nihil allatum intellego.
pairs.question: Cui deae nuptias parari Staphyla in Aulularia iocatur, quia nihil temeti allatum est?
pairs.question_en: For which goddess does Staphyla in the Aulularia joke the wedding is being prepared, since no wine has been brought?
pairs.derivation: Rite-specific joke: a 'wedding for Ceres' would be wineless, since Ceres' rites excluded wine (temetum, the archaic word for it) — Roman sacral knowledge evidenced by the joke's own logic. One-name answer verbatim; speaker tags stripped.

pairs.source_text: festo die si quid prodegeris, profesto egere liceat, nisi peperceris.
pairs.question: Quid ei licebit profesto die, qui festo die prodegerit, secundum proverbium apud Plautum in Aulularia?
pairs.question_en: What will he be free to do on the working day who has squandered on the feast day, according to the proverb in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: Proverb of thrift built on the Roman calendar division of dies festi and profesti: waste on the holiday, want on the workday. Point checkable, quoted verbatim; one-word answer.

pairs.source_text: nunc tusculum emi hoc et coronas floreas: haec imponentur in foco nostro Lari, ut fortunatas faciat gnatae nuptias.
pairs.question: Cui deo Euclio tusculum et coronas floreas in foco imposuit, ut gnatae nuptias fortunaret?
pairs.question_en: To which god did Euclio offer a bit of incense and flower garlands on the hearth, to bless his daughter's wedding?
pairs.derivation: Wedding-day domestic rite: incense and garlands laid on the hearth for the Lar to prosper the marriage — the household cult at the heart of the play. Anchored to Euclio + the Lar; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Apollo, quaeso, subveni mi atque adiuva, confige sagittis fures thensaurarios
pairs.question: Quem deum Euclio invocat, ut fures thensaurarios sagittis configat, apud Plautum?
pairs.question_en: Which god does Euclio invoke to pierce the treasure-thieves with arrows, in Plautus?
pairs.derivation: Apollo the archer — his canonical attribute, the arrows — invoked against thieves. Shared divine iconography evidenced verbatim; one-name answer.

pairs.source_text: condigne etiam meus med intus gallus gallinacius, qui erat anu peculiaris, perdidit paenissume. ubi erat haec defossa, occepit ibi scalpurrire ungulis cirum circa. quid opust verbis? ita mihi pectus peracuit: capio fustem, obtrunco gallum, furem manufestarium.
pairs.question: Quod animal Euclio in Aulularia Plauti fuste obtruncavit, quia ibi ubi aurum defossum erat scalpurribat?
pairs.question_en: What animal did Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia strike dead with a club, because it was scratching where the gold was buried?
pairs.derivation: The famous comic scene: the old woman's rooster scratches over the hiding place and Euclio kills it as a 'thief caught in the act' — a set piece every reader of the play carries. Short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: neque ego umquam nisi hodie ad Bacchas veni in Bacchanal coquinatum, ita me miserum et meos discipulos fustibus male contuderunt.
pairs.question: Quo se coquinatum venisse Congrio cocus queritur, cum ab Euclione fustibus contusus fugit?
pairs.question_en: Where does the cook Congrio complain he has come to cook, as he flees cudgelled by Euclio?
pairs.answer_en: To the Bacchants, into a Bacchic shrine.
pairs.derivation: The Bacchanal as shared byword for violent frenzy — Congrio can only compare the miser's house to cooking among raving Bacchae. Bacchic rites as ambient cultural knowledge; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam meo quidem animo si idem faciant ceteri opulentiores, pauperiorum filias ut indotatas ducant uxores domum, et multo fiat civitas concordior
pairs.question: Qualis fieret civitas, si opulentiores pauperum filias indotatas ducerent, secundum Megadorum apud Plautum?
pairs.question_en: What would the state become if the wealthier married poor men's daughters without dowries, according to Megadorus in Plautus?
pairs.derivation: Megadorus' civic argument for dowry-less marriage — the mores speech the run instructions flag as a goldmine on Roman dowry debate. One-word comparative answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ego faxim muli, pretio qui superant equos, sint viliores Gallicis cantheriis.
pairs.question: Quae iumenta pretio equos superare Megadorus in Aulularia Plauti dicit?
pairs.question_en: Which beasts of burden does Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia say exceed horses in price?
pairs.derivation: Roman market realia: mules — the carriage animals of wealthy matrons — actually outpriced horses, which is the premise of Megadorus' threat to cheapen them below Gallic geldings. One-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Dromo, desquama piscis. tu, Machaerio, congrum, murenam exdorsua quantum potest.
pairs.question: Quos duos pisces Machaerio exdorsuare iubetur in cena nuptiali apud Plautum in Aulularia?
pairs.question_en: Which two fish is Machaerio ordered to fillet for the wedding dinner in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.answer_en: The conger eel and the moray.
pairs.derivation: Named dishes of the Roman festive table: conger and murena, the prestige fish (the murena a Roman delicacy), being dressed for the wedding feast. Two-item answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam quae indotata est, ea in potestate est viri; dotatae mactant et malo et damno viros.
pairs.question: In cuius potestate esse uxorem indotatam Megadorus in Aulularia Plauti dicit?
pairs.question_en: In whose power does Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia say the undowered wife is?
pairs.derivation: The point of the whole dowry debate stated as a maxim: the undowered wife is in the husband's power, the dowered wife ruins him. Roman marriage mores (potestas/manus language) verbatim; short answer.

pairs.source_text: qui mi intro misti in aedis quingentos coquos, cum senis manibus, genere Geryonaceo
pairs.question: Cuius monstri generi Euclio coquos senis manibus praeditos adsimulat apud Plautum?
pairs.question_en: To what monster's breed does Euclio liken the cooks endowed with six hands apiece, in Plautus?
pairs.derivation: Geryon the triple-bodied giant (hence six hands) — canonical myth-figure invoked in Euclio's hyperbole about the thieving cooks. Anchored to Euclio + Geryon; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quos si Argus servet, qui oculeus totus fuit, quem quondam Ioni Iuno custodem addidit, is numquam servet.
pairs.question: Quem custodem Iuno quondam Ioni addidit, ut in Aulularia Plauti memoratur?
pairs.question_en: What guardian did Juno once set over Io, as recalled in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: Canonical myth as shared story: Argus the all-eyed watcher whom Juno appointed to guard Io — cited casually as ambient knowledge. Names and attribute all verbatim; short answer.

pairs.source_text: praeterea tibicinam, quae mi interbibere sola, si vino scatat, Corinthiensem fontem Pirenam potest.
pairs.question: Cuius urbis fons erat Pirena, ut apud Plautum in Aulularia dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Of what city was Pirene the spring, as said in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: The famous spring Pirene at Corinth — shared Greek-Roman geography, the standard of the joke that the flute-girl could drink it dry. One-place answer verbatim (Corinthiensem fontem Pirenam).

pairs.source_text: quin exta inspicere in sole ei vivo licet: ita is pellucet quasi lanterna Punica.
pairs.question: Cui rei Euclio agnum macrum pellucentem in Aulularia Plauti comparat?
pairs.question_en: To what does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia compare the scrawny lamb you can see through?
pairs.answer_en: To a Punic lantern (of translucent horn).
pairs.derivation: Realia of trade: the 'Punic lantern' of thin translucent horn, proverbially see-through — a Carthaginian import familiar enough to carry the joke. Short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ego, nisi quid me vis, eo lavatum, ut sacruficem.
pairs.question: Quid Megadorus in Aulularia Plauti prius facit, quam sacrificet?
pairs.question_en: What does Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia do before he sacrifices?
pairs.derivation: Ritual purity before sacrifice: one washes first (so too Euclio, 'nunc lavabo, ut rem divinam faciam'). Roman sacral custom evidenced verbatim; short answer.

pairs.source_text: nunc hoc mihi factu est optumum, ut ted auferam, aula, in Fidei fanum: ibi abstrudam probe.
pairs.question: In cuius deae fanum Euclio aulam auri e domo sublatam primum abstrusit?
pairs.question_en: In which goddess's shrine did Euclio first hide the pot of gold taken from his house?
pairs.derivation: The cult of Fides with her fanum — Roman deified abstraction — chosen by the miser with the running pun on fides/trust ('fretus tua, Fides, fiducia'). Anchored to Euclio + the aula; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nunc hoc ubi abstrudam cogito solum locum. Silvani lucus extra murum est avius, crebro salicto oppletus. ibi sumam locum. certumst, Silvano potius credam quam Fide.
pairs.question: Quo Euclio aulam auri, e fano Fidei ablatam, deinde abstrusit apud Plautum?
pairs.question_en: Where did Euclio then hide the pot of gold he had removed from the shrine of Fides, in Plautus?
pairs.answer_en: In the grove of Silvanus outside the wall.
pairs.derivation: Silvanus the extra-urban woodland god, his lonely grove outside the wall — Roman religion's topography, and the site of the fateful theft. Anchored to Euclio + Fides/Silvanus; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Non temere est quod corvos cantat mihi nunc ab laeva manu; semul radebat pedibus terram et voce croccibat sua
pairs.question: A qua parte corvus Euclioni cecinit, quod omen ille non temere esse putavit?
pairs.question_en: On which side did the raven croak at Euclio, an omen he thought not without meaning?
pairs.derivation: Roman bird-omen lore: the raven's cry on the left as a significant sign (Euclio later credits it with saving him: 'ni subvenisset corvos'). Augural realia verbatim; short answer.

pairs.source_text: sed si repperero, o Fides, mulsi congialem plenam faciam tibi fideliam. id adeo tibi faciam; verum ego mihi bibam, ubi id fecero.
pairs.question: Quid Strobilus deae Fidei se daturum vovet, si aurum reppererit, apud Plautum?
pairs.question_en: What does Strobilus vow to give the goddess Fides if he finds the gold, in Plautus?
pairs.answer_en: A gallon-jar (congius-sized pot) full of honey-wine (mulsum).
pairs.derivation: A comic votum with real furniture: mulsum (honey-wine) as offering, the congius measure, the fidelia jar — and the punchline that he'll drink it himself. Vow-practice realia; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Perii, mea nutrix. obsecro te, uterum dolet. Iuno Lucina, tuam fidem!
pairs.question: Quam deam filia Euclionis parturiens in Aulularia Plauti invocat?
pairs.question_en: Which goddess does Euclio's daughter call upon in labor in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: Juno Lucina, the Roman goddess of childbirth, invoked in the canonical birth-cry of comedy — shared religious knowledge evidenced verbatim. One-name answer.

pairs.source_text: Quid vis fieri? factum est illud: fieri infectum non potest.
pairs.question: Quid de re facta fieri non posse Lyconides in Aulularia Plauti dicit?
pairs.question_en: What does Lyconides in Plautus' Aulularia say cannot happen to a thing once done?
pairs.derivation: The proverb 'factum fieri infectum non potest' — what is done cannot be undone — a saying this scene helped make canonical (echoed by Terence). Quoted verbatim per the proverb rule.

pairs.source_text: ibo intro, ubi de capite meo sunt comitia.
pairs.question: Quid de capite suo intus haberi Lyconides in Aulularia Plauti iocatur, dum mater cum avunculo agit?
pairs.question_en: What does Lyconides in Plautus' Aulularia joke is being held indoors concerning his life, while his mother deals with his uncle?
pairs.answer_en: The comitia (the Roman voting assembly, as a capital court).
pairs.derivation: Roman institutional anachronism: the comitia that voted 'de capite' (on a citizen's life) transplanted into Greek Athens as a metaphor for the family council. One-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: hic mihi est Megadorus avonculus, meus pater fuit Antimachus, ego vocor Lyconides, mater est Eunomia.
pairs.question: Quo patre et qua matre natus est Lyconides adulescens in Aulularia Plauti?
pairs.question_en: Of what father and mother was the young Lyconides born, in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.answer_en: Of Antimachus as father and Eunomia as mother.
pairs.derivation: Lyconides' formal self-identification gives the family tree in one line: father Antimachus, mother Eunomia. Named-relation fact of the canonical play; two-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: hic mihi est Megadorus avonculus
pairs.question: Quis erat Lyconidi avunculus in Aulularia Plauti?
pairs.question_en: Who was Lyconides' maternal uncle in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: The kinship on which the plot turns: Megadorus, the girl's aged suitor, is the young lover's avunculus (mother's brother), and yields the bride to him. One-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quis me Athenis nunc magis quisquam est homo cui di sint propitii?
pairs.question: In qua urbe fabula Plauti quae Aulularia inscribitur agitur?
pairs.question_en: In what city is Plautus' play called the Aulularia set?
pairs.derivation: The nominal setting of the comedy, evidenced by Strobilus counting himself the most god-favored man 'at Athens' — the Greek frame through which the Roman realia poke. One-place answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quadrilibrem aulam auro onustam habeo. quis me est ditior?
pairs.question: Quanti ponderis erat aula auro onusta Euclionis, ut Strobilus in Aulularia gloriatur?
pairs.question_en: Of what weight was Euclio's pot laden with gold, as Strobilus boasts in the Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: The one number attached to the famous pot: a four-pounder of gold ('quadrilibrem... aulam', repeated at 821-822). Measure fact of the canonical play; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Is me nunc renuntiare repudium iussit tibi.
pairs.question: Quid Megadorus per Lyconidem Euclioni renuntiavit, nuptiis iam exornatis?
pairs.question_en: What did Megadorus have Lyconides announce to Euclio, though the wedding was already prepared?
pairs.answer_en: The repudium (formal breaking-off of the betrothal).
pairs.derivation: Roman legal institution: repudium, the formal renunciation of a sponsio-betrothal, duly 'renuntiatum' by messenger. Anchored to Megadorus + Euclio; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ut mi ignoscas eamque uxorem mihi des, ut leges iubent.
pairs.question: Quid fieri leges iubent, cum adulescens virginem vitiavit, ut Lyconides in Aulularia adfirmat?
pairs.question_en: What do the laws command to be done when a young man has violated a maiden, as Lyconides asserts in the Aulularia?
pairs.answer_en: That she be given to him as wife.
pairs.derivation: The comic-law commonplace (from Attic law, naturalized in the palliata): the seducer must marry the girl — 'ut leges iubent'. Anchored to Lyconides + Euclio's daughter; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam tua gnata peperit, decumo mense post: numerum cape
pairs.question: Quoto mense post Cereris vigilias filia Euclionis peperit, ut Lyconides apud Plautum computat?
pairs.question_en: In what month after the vigil of Ceres did Euclio's daughter give birth, as Lyconides reckons in Plautus?
pairs.derivation: The Roman ten-month reckoning of pregnancy ('decumo mense post: numerum cape'), tying the birth to the Ceres-vigil assault. Number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: In arca apud me. nunc volo me emitti manu.
pairs.question: Quod praemium Strobilus servus, aula auri inventa, ab ero suo petit in Aulularia Plauti?
pairs.question_en: What reward does the slave Strobilus, having found the pot of gold, ask of his master in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: Manumissio — freedom bought with a windfall — the standing dream of the comic slave and a real Roman institution ('emitti manu'). Anchored to Strobilus + the aula; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Re omni inspecta compressoris servolus Id surpit.
pairs.question: Cuius servus aulam auri Euclionis e luco Silvani surripuit in Aulularia Plauti?
pairs.question_en: Whose slave stole Euclio's pot of gold from the grove of Silvanus in Plautus' Aulularia?
pairs.answer_en: Lyconides' — the man who had violated the girl.
pairs.derivation: The theft that breaks the miser: the ravisher's slave (Strobilus in the play) spies out the hiding place and lifts the pot. Anchored via the argumentum's 'compressoris servolus'; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: per dolum mox Euclio cum perdidisset aulam, insperato invenit laetusque natam conlocat Lyconidi.
pairs.question: Cui Euclio, aula insperato recuperata, filiam suam tandem in matrimonium conlocavit?
pairs.question_en: To whom did Euclio, having unexpectedly recovered the pot, finally give his daughter in marriage?
pairs.derivation: The resolution of the play as the ancient argumentum preserves it — the play's own final scenes are lost (the text breaks off in Act V), so the transmitted summary is the evidence; nothing invented. One-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nec noctu nec diu quietus umquam servabam eam: nunc dormiam.
pairs.question: Quid Euclio, cura auri tandem liberatus, se facturum esse dicit in fragmento Aululariae?
pairs.question_en: What does Euclio, freed at last from worry over the gold, say he will do, in a fragment of the Aulularia?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated fragment of the lost ending: the miser who watched night and day can say 'nunc dormiam' once the gold is out of his hands — the moral of the play in one word. Short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: qui mi holera cruda ponunt, hallec adduint.
pairs.question: Quod condimentum holeribus crudis addendum esse dicit fragmentum Aululariae Plauti?
pairs.question_en: What condiment does a fragment of Plautus' Aulularia say should be supplied with raw vegetables?
pairs.derivation: Staple table realia: hallec/allec, the sediment of garum, as the dressing owed to a dish of raw greens — the fish-sauce family the guidelines flag as core food culture. One-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: pro illis corcotis, strophiis, sumptu uxorio
pairs.question: Quae duo vestimenta muliebria fragmentum Aululariae inter sumptum uxorium numerat?
pairs.question_en: Which two articles of women's wear does a fragment of the Aulularia count among a wife's expenses?
pairs.derivation: Dress realia from the dowry-tirade tradition: the crocota (saffron robe) and strophium as typical items of wifely luxury. Two-item answer verbatim.
